    <item>
        <title>[$] Python's experimental JIT to be removed</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102102/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102102/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p>Python's <a
href="https://docs.python.org/3.13/whatsnew/3.13.html#an-experimental-just-in-time-jit-compiler">experimental
just-in-time (JIT) compiler</a>, which was added to CPython in 2024 for the <a
href="https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-3130/">3.13&#160;release</a>,
is on its way out. In June, the Python steering council <a
href="https://discuss.python.org/t/an-announcement-from-the-steering-council-regarding-the-jit-project/107638">announced</a>
that it was pausing work on the JIT in CPython's main branch until there was an
accepted <a href="https://peps.python.org/pep-0001">Python Enhancement
Proposal</a> (PEP) that addressed concerns about maintenance, compatibility, and
set clear success metrics as well as a timeline for completion. After creating
<a href="https://peps.python.org/pep-0836/">PEP&#160;836</a> ("JIT Go Brrr: The
Path to a Supported JIT Compiler for CPython")
to try to meet the council's request, and after months of discussion, the
JIT maintainers have withdrawn the PEP. For now, it appears that development on
the once-promising project has come to an end.</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 15:45:58 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

        <item>
        <title>Systemd adds support for components written in Rust</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102970/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102970/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p>Christian Brauner has <a
href="https://mastodon.social/@brauner/117494833311192688">announced</a> that he
has <a href="https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/44324">merged support</a>
for writing leaf components of systemd in Rust. Rust will be used only for new
leaf components, existing code is not being ported to Rust and nothing that
other components depend on is written in Rust.</p>

<p>Brauner <a
href="https://mastodon.social/@brauner/117494833657858840">said</a> that the
project would like to move forward with Rust support in core systemd, "<q>but
there are several blockers in Rust's support for dynamic libraries which
prevents us from doing that without massively bloating every binary we
build</q>". Assuming all goes well, it seems likely this work will appear in the
systemd v263 release expected in December.</p>

<p></description>
        <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 15:13:59 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

        <item>
        <title>[$] The first part of the 7.4 merge window</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1101211/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1101211/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
Since the merge window for 7.4 opened, there have been 6,753 non-merge
changesets pulled into the mainline repository. Many more are expected,
especially given the possibility that this merge window will be extended to
three weeks. Still, even this initial set brought in a number of new features,
in addition to the continued general cleanups and security fixes that the kernel
has seen recently.
</p>
</description>

        <item>
        <title>[$] Seeking smaller kernel stacks</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1100271/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1100271/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>Memory has always been a scarce resource in computing systems, but the
problem seems to have worsened recently.  In particular, the worldwide
shortage of memory chips has led to a renewed focus by systems developers
on reducing memory usage.  During the memory-management microconference at
the 2026 <a href="https://lpc.events/">Linux Plumbers Conference</a>, Will
Deacon discussed one specific consumer of memory that is being
re-examined: kernel stacks.
</description>
        <pubDate>Fri, 23 Oct 2026 14:59:24 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

        <item>
        <title>[$] The end of __get_user() and __put_user()</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102061/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102061/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>Linus Torvalds rarely writes significant amounts of kernel code these days, so
the <a
href="https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/commit/?id=22a78a25438d">merging</a>
of a 48-part patch series from him is an unusual event.  This series,
destined for the 7.4 kernel release, performs some long-delayed kernel
cleanup by removing a couple of the primitives used to access user-space memory
from the kernel.  What was once a best practice has long been superseded,
but it can take time for such changes to work their way through a body of
code this large.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 22 Oct 2026 16:25:50 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>KeePassXC 2.8.0 released</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102270/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102270/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p><a href="https://keepassxc.org/blog/2026-10-21-2.8.0-released/">Version
2.8.0</a> of the <a href="https://keepassxc.org/">KeePassXC</a> password-management application has been
released.</p>

<blockquote class="bq">
The new release brings a lot of long-awaited new features, many bugfixes, and
several security updates. Among the major features are the migration from Qt5 to
Qt6, Auto-Type on Wayland (Linux), configurable keyboard shortcuts, remote
database synchronization with external tools, quick unlock with password on
macOS, and quick unlock via Polkit on Linux. Version 2.8.0 is also the first
version for which we ship native ARM64 builds for Windows and an experimental
AArch64 (i.e., ARM64) AppImage for Linux.
</blockquote>

<p>See the <a
href="https://github.com/keepassxreboot/keepassxc/releases/tag/2.8.0">changelog</a>
for a full list of new features, major changes, and bug fixes.</p></description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 22 Oct 2026 13:34:37 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>[$] Rust features in the future</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1099606/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1099606/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
There are several Rust features that kernel developers have been hoping to
stabilize, but Josh Triplett wanted to describe all of the <em>other</em>
features that the Rust project is currently working on. He spoke about the topic
at Kangrejos 2026, leaving the assembled kernel developers with several ideas
about how to use these upcoming Rust features in the kernel.
The features included refinements to the type system, small syntax improvements, and a
smarter borrow checker.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 22 Oct 2026 13:19:56 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

        <item>
        <title>Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security (PHP Foundation)</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102060/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102060/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>The PHP Foundation has put out <a
href="https://thephp.foundation/blog/2026/10/21/todays-php-security-release-and-how-were-strengthening-php-security/">a
blog entry</a> explaining how the vulnerabilities disclosed today came
about and why they took so long to fix.
<p>
<blockquote class="bq">
	To fix the OOM problem, the PHP security team developed several
	competing approaches, but each came with its own trade-offs:
	backward compatibility breaks, new denial-of-service potential, or
	requiring changes to many third-party extensions which seemed
	impossible to coordinate. The PHP security team, operating on
	consensus, struggled to choose between these and feared the
	repercussions of shipping the wrong choice. Combined with the lack
	of a known path to remote code execution and the small team of core
	developers with the necessary deep knowledge of the engine occupied
	with many responsibilities, this decision process caused work on a
	fix to stall and restart repeatedly over months. We won't pretend
	otherwise: the delay was a structural failure, caused by both the
	security team's decision process and its lack of resources.
</blockquote></description>
        <pubDate>Wed, 21 Oct 2026 20:20:34 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>More vulnerabilities in widely deployed software</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102044/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102044/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
The Node.js project has
<a
href="https://nodejs.org/en/blog/vulnerability/october-2026-security-releases">released
a number of security updates</a> to fix, among other vulnerabilities, a
remote-code-execution bug affecting programs that use Brotli compression. And,
in case any programmers who use compiled languages thought they could relax, the
<a href="https://musl.libc.org/">musl libc project</a> has also announced a
new vulnerability: an
<a
href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/20261021154307.GA4413%40brightrain.aerifal.cx/">out-of-bounds
write</a> that could potentially lead to remote code execution, although that
has not been demonstrated.
</p></description>
        <pubDate>Wed, 21 Oct 2026 17:09:24 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>[$] Hash-based module integrity for reproducible distributions</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1100026/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1100026/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jake</dc:creator>
        <description>We last looked in on <a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1012946/">hash-based integrity
checking for kernel modules</a> just over a year and half ago.  Since that time,
the <a
href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/20260505-module-hashes-v5-0-e174a5a49fce@weissschuh.net/">patch
set</a> has undergone multiple revisions.  At the 2026 <a href="https://lpc.events/">Linux Plumbers Conference</a>
(LPC),  Thomas Weißschuh described the need for kernel-module integrity
guarantees while still providing reproducible builds, how his patches implement that, and some ideas for possible
further work.
</description>
        <pubDate>Wed, 21 Oct 2026 16:14:55 +0000</pubDate>
